name: Gimlet-Reach
description: Gimlet-Reach is a robust terrestrial world with a piercing quality to its landscape, every feature sharp and defined under a clear azure sky. Mountain ranges of dark granite rise in serrated ridges that puncture the cloud layer, their peaks permanently snow-capped and their flanks dense with coniferous forest. A massive ancient crater in the northern hemisphere has filled with water over geological time, creating a perfectly circular inland sea three hundred kilometers across, its depth still unmeasured.

The higher gravity lends a grounding quality to every experience on Gimlet-Reach; visitors describe feeling more connected to the earth, more solid, more present. The air is cold and sharp at altitude, sweet with conifer resin in the valleys, and carries the calls of predatory avians whose wingspans exceed four meters. Seasons change dramatically, with long winters that bury the lowlands in meters of snow and brief, explosive summers when the forests bloom in riots of purple and gold.

A colonial settlement of approximately forty thousand inhabitants occupies the crater sea's eastern shore, established three generations ago and now largely self-sustaining. The colonists have discovered monolithic structures of unknown origin buried in the forest at regular intervals, forming a grid pattern that extends across the primary continent. The structures are inert and apparently solid, composed of a material harder than diamond, and their purpose remains entirely unknown despite decades of study.

Gimlet-Reach has become a model for successful colonization, but the monolithic grid adds an undercurrent of unease to the settlers' lives. The structures show no signs of deterioration and resist all attempts at sampling or analysis. Animals avoid them, and the forest grows thin in their immediate vicinity, as though even the trees find them uncomfortable. The colonists have learned to live with the mystery, but each new structure uncovered by forest clearing reminds them that they may not be the first to reach this world, and that the first arrivals may have left their markers for a reason.
